items.title: Eric Alexander interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010
items.q: the first instructor I had in the small group ensemble was Harold Mabern... Playing with Harold? I mean if you don’t bring your A game and really step up, he going over, it’s like a tsunami.

ctx.x: You had mentioned yesterday your father listening to you practice, and can’t you play a song all the way through or something. Did you win them over, your parents, with your dedication?

I don’t think my parents really ever knew until later how dedicated I was. Because I think the proof is really in the pudding. And I wasn’t living with them. I was far away from home when this started to happen to me. You know I had periods of time in high school where I would prepare very diligently for a saxophone recital, classical saxophone, I would learn a piece and make big strides and have some effective practice moments. So they knew I was talented. You know all of the teachers would tell them, oh your…
He must have recognized something in you.

items.title: Harold Mabern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010
items.q: Harold has enjoyed a long tenure as an instructor at William Paterson University and he records frequently with saxophonist Eric Alexander, one of his notable students.

ctx.x: Did you hear blues a lot growing up in the home?

We heard it in the home, and when I started getting into music, which was around the age of 15 or 16, see I’m a late bloomer, you know because being a self-taught musician I never took piano lessons. We had to play the blues because that was the way it was. And we were drugged and we were disappointed because we wanted to play bebop. And the club owners would say no, no, you’ve got to get that bebop out of here, you’re running my customers out of here, in other words we had to play music that they could dance to.…

we would play the blues, say “The Hucklebuck,” which you later found out was “Now’s The Time,” but it’s really “The Hucklebuck,” Paul Williams “Hucklebuck” [scats]. So we would tell the drummer, you know, keep the backbeat while the people would dance. And then, once we got them dancing, we started playing the chord changes to “All the Things You Are,” or “Perdido.” That’s how we got over.
